science.title: A strain-aware electromechanical framework for III-nitride axial nanowire heterostructures toward an energy-efficient high-frequency tunnel FET
science.description: A polarization-engineered III-nitride nanowire tunnel field-effect transistor (TFET) is investigated for low-energy, high-frequency operation under strain relaxation. Unlike approaches that optimize polarization-assisted tunneling primarily from an electrical perspective, the proposed framework introduces mechanical strain retention and critical structural dimensions as explicit constraints before electrical optimization. A coupled Wentzel–Kramers–Brillouin tunneling analysis and finite-element electromechanical framework evaluates multiple heterostructures in terms of critical thickness, strain relaxation, polarization degradation, and tunneling strength. The InN/In$$_{0.65}$$Ga$$_{0.35}$$N/InN axial nanowire is identified as a balanced structure with strong tunneling under both coherent and relaxed strain conditions. Device simulations show steep switching with a subthreshold swing of 11.3 mV/dec at 300 K, suppressed leakage, and transconductance of 723–997 $$\upmu $$S over 225–400 K. Femtofarad-scale gate capacitance enables cutoff frequencies of 268–76 GHz, indicating potential for millimeter-wave operation. Zero-bias rectification is enabled by polarization-induced built-in electric fields, which enhance band-to-band tunneling without an externally applied DC bias. The device exhibits high intrinsic gain, low noise, and high power gain across the Ka-, V-, and early W-band ranges. System-level operation is validated using a non-quasi-static compact model for a differential power detector with high-responsivity drain-biased detection and polarization-driven zero-bias rectification, demonstrating strain-aware polarization control for strain-tolerant millimeter-wave TFET operation.

science.title: Luminal geometry and coiled coil length determine submembrane localization of type II transmembrane Golgi proteins
science.description: We previously showed that transmembrane proteins laterally partition within Golgi cisternae: trafficking components (e.g., GPP130, a type II transmembrane protein) are enriched at the cisternal rim, whereas Golgi enzymes localize to the cisternal interior. However, the underlying mechanism was unclear. We found that the luminal juxtamembrane coiled coil of GPP130 is necessary and sufficient for rim localization, with coiled coil length, rather than sequence identity, determining partitioning. When retargeted to the ER, GPP130 preferentially localized to ER sheet rims and was partially excluded from the nuclear envelope, an exclusion reduced upon nuclear envelope expansion. Cryo-electron tomography revealed that the intraluminal widths of Golgi cisternal interiors, some ER sheets, and the nuclear envelope are smaller than the predicted coiled coil length. Two additional type II Golgi transmembrane proteins with long luminal juxtamembrane coiled coils similarly localized to cisternal rims. These findings identify intraluminal width as a mechanism governing the lateral partitioning of type II transmembrane proteins with long luminal coiled coils. Wong et al. show that the intraluminal widths of the ER and Golgi and the length of luminal coiled coils of the transmembrane proteins determine localization, revealing a geometry-based localization mechanism.
